passage:
Bidisha was nine when she got stuck on the word "enormous" in front of the whole class. Her ears went hot. Instead of trying again, she crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and read the next line in a squeaky voice. The class burst out laughing, and Asif Sir hid a smile before asking her to read properly. Bidisha grinned around at everyone, but her hands were shaking against the book.
At fifteen she still reached for a joke when her stomach dropped. After a group project went missing, she texted her friend Uday: "Great, just great 🙂". Uday stared at the screen. Was she angry, or being funny? Her flat voice in class the next day gave him no clue either. He nudged her at lunch. "Are you joking, or are you actually upset?" Bidisha let out a breath. "Upset. I was hoping you'd ask." She pushed her tray aside and told him about the lost files.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do after she got stuck on the word "enormous"?
qa.a: She crossed her eyes, puffed out her cheeks and read the next line in a squeaky voice.

qa.q: How are Bidisha's squeaky reading at nine and her "Great, just great" text at fifteen alike, and how do they differ in how others take them?
qa.a: Both are jokes she uses to cover worry. At nine the class saw a silly face and laughed, but at fifteen the sarcasm was flat and in text, so Uday could not tell whether she was angry or being funny until he asked.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when she grinned at the class with shaking hands?
qa.a: She was embarrassed and anxious. The grin showed she wanted to stay in charge of the moment, while the trembling hands showed the worry underneath.

qa.q: What could Uday do when someone's sarcastic message leaves him unsure?
qa.a: He can ask a plain, kind question, like "Are you joking, or are you actually upset?", and then really listen to the answer.

grounding: A joke used to cover embarrassment at nine (3891) becomes sarcasm at fifteen (2581) that is easily misread, so a clarifying question helps.
